'''''Phytolacca americana''''', also known as '''American pokeweed''', '''pokeweed''', '''poke sallet''', '''pokeberry''', '''dragonberries''', '''pigeonberry weed''', and '''inkberry''', is a poisonous, [[herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]] in the pokeweed family [[Phytolaccaceae]]. This pokeweed grows {{convert|4 to 10|ft|m|order=flip|sigfig=1}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/phytolacca-americana/|title = Phytolacca americana (American Pokeweed, Common Pokeweed, Garnet, Pidgeon Berry, Poke, Pokeberry, Pokeweed, Scoke) | North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|website=Plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref> It has simple leaves on green to red or purplish stems and a large white [[taproot]]. The flowers are green to white, followed by berries which ripen through red to purple to almost black which are a food source for songbirds such as [[grey catbird|gray catbird]], [[northern mockingbird]], [[northern cardinal]], and [[brown thrasher]], as well as other birds and some small non-avian animals (i.e., for species that are unaffected by its mammalian [[toxin]]s).
[[File:American pokeweed (lat. Phytolacca americana).jpg|thumb|American pokeweed (lat. ''Phytolacca americana'')]]
Pokeweed is native to eastern [[North America]], the Midwest, and the South, with more scattered populations in the far West where it was introduced.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://legacy.tropicos.org/NamePage.aspx?nameid=50202801&projectid=23 | title=Tropicos | Name - Phytolacca americana L. Var. Americana|website=Legacy.tropicos.org }}</ref> It is also naturalized in parts of Europe and Asia. It is considered a pest species by farmers.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ucanr.edu/blogs/blogcore/postdetail.cfm?postnum=27983|date=August 15, 2018|title=Pokeweed: A giant of a weed!|first=Scott|last=Oneto|publisher=Agriculture and Natural Resources, University of California}}</ref> Pokeweed is poisonous to humans, dogs, and livestock. In spring and early summer, shoots and leaves (not the root) are edible with proper cooking (hence the common name "poke sallet"),<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ucanr.edu/blogs/blogcore/postdetail.cfm?postnum=27983|title=Pokeweed: A giant of a weed!|website=ANR Blogs}}</ref> but later in the summer they become poisonous, and the berries are also poisonous. It is used as an ornamental in horticulture, and it provokes interest for the variety of its natural products (toxins and other classes), for its ecological role, its historical role in traditional medicine, and for some utility in biomedical research (e.g., in studies of [[pokeweed mitogen]]). In the wild, it is easily found growing in pastures, recently cleared areas, and woodland openings, [[edge habitat]]s such as along [[fencerow]]s, and in wastelands.

==Description==
[[File:Pokeberries.png |thumb|Pokeweed berries]]
[[File:Mature Pokeweed.jpg|thumb]]
Pokeweed is a member of the family [[Phytolaccaceae]], and is a large herbaceous perennial plant,<ref name=Owen88/> growing up to {{Convert|2.5|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} in height over the course of a summer.<ref name=Owen88/> One to several branches grow from the crown of a thick, white, fleshy [[taproot]]; Michael D. K. Owen describes the branches as "stout, smooth, [and] green to somewhat purplish". Simple, entire leaves with long petioles are alternately arranged along the stem.<ref name=Owen88/>

Pokeweeds reproduce only by their large, glossy black, lens-shaped seeds, which are contained in a fleshy, 10-celled, purple-to-near-black berry that has crimson juice. The flowers are [[perfect flower|perfect]], [[Symmetry in biology#Radial symmetry|radially symmetric]], white or green, with 4–5 sepals and no petals. The flowers develop in elongated clusters termed [[racemes]].<ref name=Owen88/><ref>Each flower has 10 stamens and a 10-cell pistil and gives rise to a 10-celled berry</ref> The seeds have long viability, able to germinate after many years in the soil.

=== Morphology ===
{{more citations needed section |date=September 2016}}
[[File:Phytolacca americana 004.JPG|thumb|upright|A cluster of unripe pokeweed berries]]
[[File:Phytolacca_americana_cluster_-_single.jpg|thumb|upright|A cluster of ripe pokeweed berries]]

''Plant Type'': Perennial herbaceous plant which can reach a height of {{Convert|3|m|abbr=on|frac=2}}<ref name="Elias-2009">{{Cite book |last1=Elias |first1=Thomas S. |title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods |last2=Dykeman |first2=Peter A. |publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]] |year=2009 |isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9 |location=New York |pages=96, 267 |oclc=244766414 |orig-date=1982}}</ref> but is usually {{Convert|1.2 to 2|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}}. The plant must be a few years old before the root grows large enough to support this size. The stem is usually red late in the season. There is an upright, erect central stem early in the season, which changes to a spreading, horizontal form later with the weight of the berries. The plant dies back to the roots each winter. The stem has a chambered [[pith]].

''Leaves'': The leaves are alternate with coarse texture with moderate [[porosity]]. Leaves can reach {{Convert|16|in|cm|abbr=off|order=flip}} in length. Each leaf is entire. Leaves are medium green and smooth, with a distinct odor that many characterize as unpleasant.

''Flowers'': The flowers have 5 regular parts with upright stamens and are up to {{convert |5|mm|frac=4}} wide. They have white petal-like sepals without true petals, on white pedicels and peduncles in an upright or drooping raceme, which darken as the plant fruits. Blooms first appear in early summer and continue into early fall.

''Fruit'': A shiny dark purple berry held in [[raceme|racemose]] clusters on pink [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]]s with a pink [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]]. Pedicels without berries have a distinctive rounded five part calyx. Fruits are round with a flat indented top and bottom. Immature berries are green, turning white and then blackish purple.

''Root'': Thick central taproot which grows deep and spreads horizontally. Rapid growth. Tan cortex, white pulp, moderate number of rootlets. Transversely cut root slices show concentric rings. No nitrogen fixation ability.<ref name="GRIN" />{{failed verification |date=May 2015}}<ref name="autogenerated1">Anon., 2015, "Entry: ''Phytolacca americana'' – L.," at ''Plants For A Future'' (organizational webpage), see [http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Phytolacca+americana], accessed 2 May 2015.</ref>{{better source needed |date=May 2015}}

Nat. Prod. |volume=43 |issue=4 |pages=510–3 |doi=10.1021/np50010a013 |bibcode=1980JNAtP..43..510K }}</ref> as well as the [[saponins]] [[phytolaccaside]]s A, B, D, E, and G, and [[phytolaccasaponin]]s B, E, and G (in the roots).<ref name="Suga1978">{{cite journal|last1=Suga |first1=Y. |last2=Maruyama |first2=Y. |last3=Kawanishi |first3=S. |last4=Shoji |first4=J. |year=1978 |title=Studies on the constituents of phytolaccaceous plants. I. On the structures of phytolaccasaponin B, E and G from the roots of ''Phytolacca americana'' L |journal=Chem. Pharm. Bull. |volume=26 |issue=2 |pages=520–5 |doi=10.1248/cpb.26.520 |doi-access=free |bibcode=1978ChPB...26..520S }}</ref><ref>{{cite book | author1 = Tang, W. | author2 = Eisenbrand, G. | date = 1992 | title = Chinese Drugs of Plant Origin: Chemistry, Pharmacology, and Use in Traditional and Modern Medicine | location = New York, NY | publisher = Springer-Verlag | page = 765 }}</ref>

The roots also contain other triterpenoids such as [[oleanolic acid]], [[spinasterol|α-spinasterol]] and its [[glucoside]], α-spinasteryl-β-<small>D</small>-glucoside, and a [[palmitoylation|palmityl]]-derivative, 6-palmytityl-α-spinasteryl-6-<small>D</small>-glucoside, as well as a similarly functionalized [[stigmasterol]] derivative, 6-palmityl-Δ7-stigmasterol-Δ-<small>D</small>-glucoside.<ref name="Suga1978" /> Pokeweed berries also contain [[betalain]] pigments such as [[betanin]] and others.<ref name="Iwashina2009">{{Cite journal |last1=Iwashina |first1=T. |last2=Kitajima |first2=J. |date=2009 |title=Flavonoids from the leaves of betalain-containing species, Phytolacca americana (Phytolaccaceae). |url=https://www.cabdirect.org/cabdirect/abstract/20123009710 |journal=Bulletin of the National Museum of Nature and Science. Series B, Botany |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=99–104 |issn=1881-9060 |access-date=2020-10-18}}</ref> The leaves contain a number of common flavonols.<ref name="Iwashina2009" /> Seeds of pokeweed contain the phenolic aldehyde [[caffeic aldehyde]].<ref>Woo, W.S., Kang, S.S., 1979. A new phenolic aldehyde from the seeds of phytolacca americana. Soul Taehakkyo Saengyak Yonguso Opjukjip 18, 30–31.</ref> 

Pokeweed also contains [[lectin]]s, such as [[pokeweed mitogen]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bekeredjian-Ding |first1=Isabelle |last2=Foermer |first2=Sandra |last3=Kirschning |first3=Carsten J. |last4=Parcina |first4=Marijo |last5=Heeg |first5=Klaus |date=2012-01-04 |title=Poke Weed Mitogen Requires Toll-Like Receptor Ligands for Proliferative Activity in Human and Murine B Lymphocytes |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=7 |issue=1 |article-number=e29806 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0029806|pmid=22238657 |pmc=3251602 |bibcode=2012PLoSO...729806B |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Etymology==
The first word in its scientific name, ''Phytolacca americana'', comes from the Greek words {{transliteration|grc|phyton}} ('plant') and {{transliteration|grc|[[Lac (resin)|lac]]ca}}—the scarlet dye secreted by the ''[[Kerria lacca]]'' scale insect. The second denotes this plant as native to America.  The common name "poke" is derived from ''puccoon'', ''pocan'', or ''poughkone'' (from an [[Algonquin peoples|Algonquin]] name for the plant).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nybg.org/content/uploads/2017/08/EcoQuest_September2017_Pokeweed_Info_Final.pdf|title=Phytolacca americana L. American Pokeweed Family|website=New York Botanical Garden}}</ref> Its berries were once used to make ink, hence its other sometimes-used common name, inkberry.

== Distribution and habitat ==
Pokeweed is native to eastern [[North America]], the Midwest, the [[Gulf Coast]], and the West Coast of the US.<ref>{{cite web |title=Plant Profile:''Phytolacca americana'' L., American pokeweed |url=https://plants.sc.egov.usda.gov/plant-profile/PHAM4 |access-date=16 November 2017 |publisher=[[USDA]] Natural Resources Conservation Service: PLANTS Database}}</ref> It is an introduced weed in [[Japan]].

== Ecology ==
Birds are unaffected by the poisons in the berries,<ref name="Owen88" /> and eat them, dispersing the seeds. The berries are reported to be a good food source for songbirds and other bird species and small animals that are unaffected by its toxins.<ref name="MatthewsGOV87">Nancy L. Matthews, 1987, "Appendix F: Hab
itat Assessment Manual," in ''Report: Anne Arundel Co., Offc. Planning and Zoning, Environmental and Special Projects Div., to Office of Coastal Resources Management, NOAA and State of Maryland Chesapeake Bay Critical Area Commission,'' August 1987, 9 pages, ''passim'' see [https://www.gpo.gov/fdsys/pkg/CZIC-qh352-m38-1987/html/CZIC-qh352-m38-1987.htm], accessed 2 May 2015.</ref> Distribution via birds is thought to account for the appearance of isolated plants in areas otherwise free from pokeweed.<ref name="Owen88" />

Pokeweed berries are reported to be a good food source for songbirds such as [[grey catbird|gray catbird]] (''Dumetella carolinensis''), [[northern mockingbird]] (''Mimus polyglottos''), [[northern cardinal]] (''Cardinalis cardinals''), [[brown thrasher]] (''Toxostoma rufum''), mourning dove (''Zenaida macroura''), and [[cedar waxwing]] (''Bombycilla cedrorum''). Small mammals apparently tolerant of its toxins include raccoon, opossum, red and gray fox, and the white-footed mouse.<ref name="MatthewsGOV87" /><ref>Other birds reported to include pokeweed in their diets include bluebirds, crested flycatchers, fish crows, hairy woodpeckers, kingbirds, phoebes, robins, starlings, and yellaw-breasted chats, see Matthews, 1987, op. cit.</ref>

Pokeweed is sometimes used as a food source by black bears.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Najar |first=Jamie |date=2020-05-15 |title=Comparison of black bear diets in eastern Oklahoma across seasons and regions |url=https://shareok.org/handle/11244/329451?show=full |journal=Shareok |page=6 |archive-date=2024-11-27 |access-date=2023-10-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241127174840/https://shareok.org/handle/11244/329451?show=full |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Pokeweed is used as a sometime food source by the larvae of some ''Lepidoptera'' species, including the [[Hypercompe scribonia|giant leopard moth]] (''Hypercompe scribonia'').<ref>Donald W. Hall, 2015, "Giant woolly bear (larva), giant or great leopard moth (adult) [scientific name: ''Hypercompe scribonia'' (Stoll 1790) (Lepidoptera: Erebidae: Arctiinae)]," at ''Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences: Featured creatures'', Gainesville, FL:Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, Division of Plant Industry, Table 1, see {{cite web |title=Giant woolly bear, great leopard moth - Hypercompe scribonia (Stoll 1790) |url=https://entnemdept.ufl.edu/creatures/MISC/MOTHS/Hypercompe_scribonia.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150920021734/http://entnemdept.ufl.edu/creatures/MISC/MOTHS/Hypercompe_scribonia.htm |archive-date=2015-09-20 |access-date=2015-05-03}}, accessed 2 May 2–15.</ref>

== Toxicity ==
All parts of the plant can be toxic and pose risks to the health of all mammals, including humans.<ref name="Owen88">{{cite journal|author=Michael D. K. Owen|year=1988|title=Pokeweed (''Phytolacca americana'' L.)|journal=Publication Pm-746 of the Iowa State University Extension Service, Ames, IA|publisher=Iowa State University|url=http://www.extension.iastate.edu/Publications/PM746.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030318002414/http://www.extension.iastate.edu/Publications/PM746.pdf|access-date=22 Oct 2025|archive-date=18 March 2003|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="oardc">{{cite journal|author1=John Cardina|author2=Cathy Herms|author3=Tim Koch|author4=Ted Webster|date=2015|title=Entry: Common Pokeweed, Phytolacca americana|journal=Ohio Perennial and Biennial Weed Guide|location=Wooster, OH|publisher=Ohio Agricultural Research and Development Center (OARDC)|url=http://www.oardc.ohio-state.edu/weedguide/singlerecord.asp?id=270|access-date=2 May 2015|archive-date=16 March 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150316234951/http://www.oardc.ohio-state.edu/weedguide/singlerecord.asp?id=270}}</ref><ref name="HellerNLM13">{{cite journal|author=Jacob L. Heller|title=Pokeweed poisoning|journal=MedlinePlus|date=October 21, 2013|url=https://www.medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002874.htm|access-date=2 May 2015}}</ref><ref name="CPPIS13">{{cite web|author=CBIF CPPIS|title=All Plants (Scientific Name): ''Phytolacca americana''|work=Canadian Biodiversity Information Facility, Species Bank, Canadian Poisonous Plants Information System|date=June 5, 2013|url=http://www.cbif.gc.ca/eng/species-bank/canadian-poisonous-plants-information-system/all-plants-scientific-name/phytolacca-americana/?id=1370403266967|access-date=2 May 2015}}</ref><ref name="Dasgupta11">{{cite book|author=Amitava Dasgupta|year=2011|title=Effects of Herbal Supplements on Clinical Laboratory Test Results|volume=2, Patient Safety|publisher=Walter de Gruyter|isbn=978-3-11-024562-2|url=https://books.google.com/books?isbn=3110245620|access-date=2 May 2015}}</ref> Toxins are found in highest concentration in the rootstock, then leaves and stems, then the ripe fruit.<ref name="oardc" /><ref name="HellerNLM13" /> The plant generally gets more toxic with maturity,<ref name="oardc" /> with the exception of the berries, which are dangerous even while green.<ref name="Dasgupta11" />

Children may be attracted by clusters of berries.<ref name=Owen88/> [[Ohio Agricultural Research and Development Center]] (OARDC) notes:<ref name="oardc"/>

{{Blockquote |1=Children are most frequently poisoned by eating raw berries. Infants are especially sensitive and have died from eating only a few raw berries. Adults have been poisoned, sometimes fatally, by eating improperly prepared leaves and shoots, especially if part of the root is harvested with the shoot, and by mistaking the root for an edible tuber. Research with humans has also shown that common pokeweed can cause mutations (possibly leading to cancer) and birth defects. Since the juice of pokeweed can be absorbed through the skin, contact of plant parts with bare skin should be avoided.}}

Pokeweed is to be avoided during pregnancy and children consuming even one berry may require emergency treatment.<ref name=autogenerated1/> The plant sap can cause [[dermatitis]] in sensitive people.<ref name=autogenerated1/>

Most mammals dislike the taste of the plant and avoid it unless it is the only food source or if it is mixed in their feed. The fresh leaves have poisoned livestock who have eaten the green leaves or roots.<ref name="oardc"/>

If death occurs, it is usually due to respiratory paralysis.<ref name=Owen88/>

Pokeweed poisoning was common in eastern North America during the 19th century, especially from the use of tinctures as antirheumatic preparations and from ingestion of berries and roots that were mistaken for [[parsnip]], [[Jerusalem artichoke]], or [[horseradish]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lewis |first1=W. H. |last2=Smith |first2=P. R. |title=Poke root herbal tea poisoning |journal=J. Am. Med. Assoc. |volume=242 |issue=25 |pages=2759–60 |date=December 1979 |pmid=501875 |doi= 10.1001/jama.242.25.2759}}</ref>

===Symptoms and response to poisoning===
Owen states:<ref name=Owen88/>

{{Blockquote |1=
If taken internally, pokeweed is a slow acting but a violent [[emetic]]. Vomiting usually starts about two hours after the plant or parts of it have been eaten. Severe cases of poisoning result in purging, spasms, and sometimes convulsions. If death occurs, it is usually due to paralysis of the respiratory organs. Cases of animal or human poisoning should be handled by a veterinarian or a physician.}}

The OARDC staff scientists note that symptoms of poisoning include "a burning sensation in the mouth, salivation, gastrointestinal cramps, and vomiting and bloody diarrhea", and that depending upon the amount consumed, more severe symptoms can occur, including "anemia, altered heart rate and respiration, convulsions and death from respiratory failure."<ref name="oardc"/> If only small quantities are ingested, people and other mammals recover within one to two days.<ref name="oardc"/><ref>One study performed in Oklahoma in 1962 concluded that the oral lethal dose of fresh poke berries in mice was about 300 gm/kg body weight and for dry berries was about 100 gm/kg body weight, and that liquid berry extract was 80 times as toxic when injected intraperitoneally as when taken orally. See {{cite journal | url=http://digital.library.okstate.edu/OAS/oas_pdf/v43/p54_57.pdf |journal=Proc. of the Okla. Acad. Of Sci. |date=1962 |pages=54–57 |title=Studies on the Toxicity of Poke Berries |last1=Ogzewalla |last2=Mossberg |last3=Beck |last4=Farrington |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181219182539/http://digital.library.okstate.edu/OAS/oas_pdf/v43/p54_57.pdf |archive-date=2018-12-19}}</ref>

==Uses==
[[File:Woman preparing poke salad.jpg|thumb|Woman preparing poke salad]]

===Horticulture===

Some pokeweeds are grown as ornamental plants, mainly for their attractive berries. A number of cultivars have been selected for larger fruit [[panicle]]s.<ref>{{cite web|title=Phytolacca americana American pokeweed|url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/12895/American-pokeweed/Details|publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=16 November 2017|date=2017|quote=White-pink flowers appear in racemes from mid-summer to early autumn, followed by crimson-black berries in autumn}}</ref>

=== Folk and alternative medicine ===

Owen notes that "Indians and early settlers used the root in poultices and certain drugs for skin diseases and rheumatism."<ref name="Owen88" />

The late 19th century herbal, the ''King's American Dispensatory,'' describes various folk medical uses that led individuals to ingest pokeberry products.<ref name="autogenerated3">John King, Harvey Wickes Felter & John Uri Lloyd, 1898, "Entry: Phytolacca," in ''King's American Dispensatory,'' Cincinnati : Ohio Valley Co., see [https://www.worldcat.org/oclc/3799356] and [http://www.henriettes-herb.com/eclectic/kings/phytolacca.html], accessed 2 May 2015.</ref> ''Phytolacca'' extract was advertised as a prescription weight loss drug in the 1890s.<ref>{{cite book |title=The Medical and surgical reporter |year=1858 |publisher=Philadelphia, Pa.: Crissy & Markley, Printers |page=1561 |edition=69th, July–Dec 1893 |url=https://archive.org/stream/medicalsurgical691893phil/medicalsurgical691893phil#page/n1560/mode/1up}}</ref>

Pokeweed is promoted in alternative medicine as a dietary supplement intended to treat a wide range of maladies including [[mumps]], [[arthritis]] and various skin conditions.<ref name="acs" /> While pokeweed has been subject to laboratory research, there is no [[evidence-based medicine|medical evidence]] that it has any beneficial effect on human health.<ref name="acs">{{cite book |publisher=[[American Cancer Society]] |title=American Cancer Society Complete Guide to Complementary and Alternative Cancer Therapies |edition=2nd |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-944235-71-3 |editor=Ades TB |pages=[https://archive.org/details/americancancerso0000unse/page/466 466–469] |chapter=Pokeweed |chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/americancancerso0000unse/page/466}}</ref>

===Food uses===
Poke is a traditional [[Appalachia|southern Appalachia]]n food. The leaves and stems of young plants can be eaten, but must be cooked by boiling two or more times with the water drained and replaced each time.<ref name="Elias-2009" /> The leaves taste similar to spinach; the stems, similar to [[asparagus]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Smith |first=Andrew |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DOJMAgAAQBAJ&pg=RA2-PA25 |title=The Oxford Encyclopedia of Food and Drink in America |date=2013-01-31 |publisher=OUP USA |isbn=978-0-19-973496-2 |language=en}}</ref> A 1917 article on edible weeds stated that pokeweed shoots were popular in Pennsylvania, "tied in small bundles, boiled the same way as asparagus, and served with cream sauce or melted butter."<ref name="LHJ1917">{{Cite magazine |title=In These Days of High Prices |last=Scott |first=Mrs. Anna B. |magazine=The Ladies' Home Journal |volume=34 |date=June 1917 |page=41 |hdl=2027/mdp.39015018052467?urlappend=%3Bseq=576 |url=https://hdl.handle.net/2027/mdp.39015018052467?urlappend=%3Bseq=576 |access-date=2024-03-07 |via=HathiTrust |language=en}}</ref>

The roots are poisonous, as are mature leaves and stems.<ref name="Elias-2009" /> Some festivals still celebrate the plant's use in its historical food preparations.

As late as the 1990s two companies commercially canned and sold pokeweed, but in 2000 the last one, the Allen Canning Company of Siloam Springs, Arkansas, closed down its operation.<ref>{{cite web|title=Pokeweed: Prime Potherb|url=http://www.eattheweeds.com/can-be-deadly-but-oh-so-delicious-pokeweed-2/|website=Eattheweeds.com|date=31 August 2011 |access-date=2024-05-20}}</ref>

=== Other uses ===
Plant toxins from ''Phytolacca'' are being explored as a means to control [[zebra mussel]]s.<ref>Harold H. Lee, Lemma Aklilu, and Harriett J. Bennett, 1992, The use of Endod (''Phytolacca dodecandra'') to Control the Zebra Mussels (''Dreissena polymorpha''), Chapter 37, pp. 643–656, in ''Zebra Mussels Biology, Impacts, and Control,'' Thomas F. Nalepa & Don W. Schloesser, Eds., Boca Raton, FL:CRC Press, {{ISBN|0873716965}}, see [https://books.google.com/books?isbn=0873716965], accessed 5 May 2015.</ref><ref>{{ cite patent |country=US |number=5252330 |status= application |title=Method of controlling zebra mussels with extract of Phytolacca dodecandra |pubdate=1993-10-12 |fdate=1993-10-12 |pridate=1993-10-12 |invent1= Harold H. Lee |invent2= Peter C. Fraleigh |invent3= Lemma Aklilu |assign1= University of Toledo.}}</ref>

The toxic extract of ripe pokeweed berries can be processed to yield a pink dye.<ref>Pesha Black & Micah Hahn, 2004, "Pokeweed, ''Phytolacca americana'', Family: Phytolaccaceae," at ''[Guide to] Practical Plants of New England (student project pages),'' see {{cite web |url=https://www.bio.brandeis.edu/fieldbio/Survival/Pages/pokeweed.html |title=Pokeweed |access-date=2015-05-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150217053151/http://www.bio.brandeis.edu/fieldbio/Survival/Pages/pokeweed.html |archive-date=2015-02-17}}, accessed 2 May 2015.</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Brooklyn Botanical Garden |title=Weed of the Month: Pokeweed |url=https://www.bbg.org/news/weed_of_the_month_pokeweed |website=www.bbg.org |access-date=23 September 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Tull |first1=Delena |title=Edible and useful plants of the Southwest : Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona: including recipes, teas and spices, natural dyes, medicinal uses, poisonous plants, fibers, basketry, and industrial uses |date=2013 |publisher=University of Texas press |isbn=978-0-292-74827-9 |page=257 |edition=Revised |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=weWQAAAAQBAJ&q=poke%20dye%20recipe&pg=PA257 |access-date=23 September 2017}}</ref> Early European settlers to North America would procure a fine red dye from the plant's roots.<ref>{{cite book|last=Kalm|first=Pehr|author-link=Pehr Kalm|title=Travels into North America: containing its natural history, and a circumstantial account of its plantations and agriculture in general, with the civil, ecclesiastical and commercial state of the country, the manners of the inhabitants, and several curious and important remarks on various subjects |publisher=T. Lowndes |year=1772|location=London|translator=Johann Reinhold Forster |pages=[https://archive.org/details/travelsintonorth01kalm_3/page/74/mode/1up 74-75] |url= |language=en|oclc=1083889360 |isbn=978-0-665-51500-2 }}</ref>

During the middle of the 19th century wine often was coloured with juice from pokeberries.<ref>Nilsson ''et al.'' 1970. "Studies into the pigments in [[beetroot]] (''Beta vulgaris'' L. ssp. ''vulgaris'' var. ''rubra'' L.)"</ref>

''Phytolacca'' contains lectins known as Pokeweed mitogen which are used to stimulate B-cell proliferation which is useful for B-cell assays, immunodeficiency diagnostic test, and immunotherapy.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bekeredjian-Ding|first1=Isabelle|last2=Foermer|first2=Sandra|last3=Kirschning|first3=Carsten J.|last4=Parcina|first4=Marijo|last5=Heeg|first5=Klaus|date=2012-01-04|title=Poke Weed Mitogen Requires Toll-Like Receptor Ligands for Proliferative Activity in Human and Murine B Lymphocytes|journal=PLOS ONE|volume=7|issue=1|article-number=e29806|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0029806|issn=1932-6203|pmc=3251602|pmid=22238657|bibcode=2012PLoSO...729806B|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Cultural significance==
===In music===
A 1969 hit written and performed by [[Tony Joe White]], "[[Polk Salad Annie]]", is about ''poke sallet'', the cooked greens-like dish made from pokeweed. The lyrics include:<ref name=Doppelbauer08fan>{{cite web |author=Doppelbauer, Martin |date=2008 |title=Tony Joe White – His Music |url=https://www.martin-doppelbauer.de/TJW/music4.htm |access-date=May 2, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150503015345/https://www.martin-doppelbauer.de/TJW/music4.htm |archive-date=May 3, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=White, Tony Joe |date=1969 |title=Polk Salad Annie [Lyrics] |location=New York, NY |publisher=Sony/ATV Music Publishing |url=http://www.metrolyrics.com/polk-salad-annie-lyrics-elvis-presley.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304095943/http://www.metrolyrics.com/polk-salad-annie-lyrics-elvis-presley.html|archive-date=2016-03-04|access-date= May 2, 2015}}</ref><blockquote>

And in the fields looks somethin' like a turnip green<br />
And everybody calls it polk salad, polk salad
</blockquote>

[[Elvis Presley]] covered the song.
